\title{``Solved'' Is a Choice of Verifier, Not a Fact:\\
Pricing, Dialing, and Routing Deterministic Verifiers, with Cost-Repair in a Real RLVR Loop}
% Double-blind: DO NOT de-anonymize until camera-ready. Camera-ready author block (for later):
%   Wenhui Chen (corresponding, wenhui.chen@inceptlabs.ai), Qingqing Mao, Chenghua Wang; InceptLabs-Shanghai.
\author{Anonymous submission}
\affiliations{Anonymous submission}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
\noindent The standard defense against reward hacking in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards
(RLVR) is to make the verifier \emph{deterministic}---executable tests, symbolic checkers, folding
oracles---on the premise that a computed verdict cannot be reward-model error. We argue determinism is
\emph{necessary but not sufficient}: a fully decidable verifier still over-accepts, because ``solved'' is
not a property of a solution but a \emph{choice of verifier}---a choice of specification and strictness that
trades cost against robustness along a frontier that is usually argued rather than measured. We contribute an
\emph{instrument} that makes the choice a controllable variable. In two deterministic domains (RNA inverse
design, SAT) a single problem admits a provably nested family of decidable predicates, priced and dial-able
from a cheap permissive proxy to an expensive strict one; we measure over-acceptance on two axes---an
out-of-domain oracle ($99.6\%$ false accepts) and a too-weak rung ($92\%$)---and reproduce the too-weak-rung
effect on a real LLM code verifier (HumanEval+, conditional false-accept $2.4\%$ strong vs.\ $28.4\%$ weak
proposer). Our central positive result treats the verifier as a \emph{priced, routable object inside a real
RLVR training loop}: running GRPO on mathematical reasoning (Qwen2.5-3B/7B, Llama-3.1-8B) with the verifier
as the sole variable, a provably sound ($\epsilon{=}0$) cheapest-first cascade attains the strong verifier's
training quality and held-out accuracy at \textbf{\mSevenBSavings\%/\longSavings\%} fewer strong-verifier
calls (7B, $800$/$2000$ steps), while the cheap reward inflates but fails to transfer---its held-out accuracy
does not rise and its gaming rate does. The routing saving is largest exactly when the policy is weakest
(early training), decaying from $\threeBSavings\%$ (3B) as capability grows. To our knowledge this is the
first treatment of the verifier as a cost-priced, continuously dial-able, sound-routable object in the RLVR
reward path.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
RLVR has moved the binding constraint of large-model training onto the \emph{verifier}
\citep{verificationhorizon,hiddencosts,lambert2024tulu3}. A reward must be \emph{cheap} to evaluate at the
scale of millions of rollouts, \emph{faithful} enough that improving it improves the objective, and
\emph{robust} enough that an optimizer cannot satisfy its letter while violating its intent. When the reward
is an imperfect proxy, optimization Goodharts the objective: models pass an \emph{extensional} check while
failing an \emph{intensional} one, and the prevalence rises with optimization pressure
\citep{gamingverifiers,rubricrewardhacking,correlatedproxies}. The common fix is to replace a learned reward
model with a \emph{deterministic} verifier, on the premise that a computed verdict has no reward-model error
to exploit \citep{verificationhorizon}.

\paragraph{Determinism is necessary but not sufficient.} A fully \emph{decidable} verifier can still be
gamed, on two orthogonal axes determinism does nothing to close: an oracle that cannot \emph{represent} the
objective (Axis~1), and a rung whose criterion is met without the property one wants (Axis~2). Consider
designing an RNA sequence folding to a target \emph{pseudoknotted} structure. The ubiquitous
minimum-free-energy (MFE) folding tool cannot represent crossing pairs at all, so a practitioner is forced
to optimize the nested \emph{skeleton}---and the tool reports ``solved'' on $250$ of $251$ natural
pseudoknots, while a pseudoknot-aware predictor finds the full target pair set in \emph{none}. The design did
not change; the \emph{verifier} did. ``Solved'' went from $99.6\%$ to nearly zero.

\paragraph{The verifiers used in practice cannot measure this.} LLM judges, learned rubric models, and
unit-test suites are \emph{noisy} (the same output gets different verdicts, confounding any weak-vs-strong
gap with evaluator variance) and \emph{not dial-able} (no knob that turns a verifier continuously from cheap
and permissive to expensive and strict while holding everything else fixed). The tension is therefore
discussed qualitatively---``stronger is better but costlier''---never quantified as a frontier one can trade
along, or optimized \emph{inside} a training loop.

\paragraph{This paper.} We build the instrument and then use it where it matters. Two \emph{deterministic}
domains (RNA, SAT) admit, per problem, a nested family of \emph{decidable} predicates whose verdict is
\emph{computed} not judged---so the verifier contributes zero conditional-verdict variance---and that can be
\emph{dialed} from a cheap proxy to a strict predicate, each with a measured cost. This lets us measure
exactly how the cheap-vs-strong acceptance gap moves with verifier strength, hardness, and optimization
pressure, and to prove and price routing policies. We then show the same object behaves as a priced, routable
reward \emph{inside} GRPO on mathematical reasoning: with the verifier as the sole independent variable, a
sound cheapest-first cascade buys the strong verifier's decisions at a fraction of its compute, and a
continuous risk-calibrated \emph{dial} traces the cost$\times$robustness frontier between a cheap and a strong
verifier. ``Solved'' is a choice; we make it a \emph{priced, dial-able, routable} one.

\paragraph{Contributions.}
\begin{itemize}\itemsep2pt
\item A deterministic, dial-able, cost-priced verifier ladder in two domains with a proved strictness nesting
and an explicit out-of-domain-oracle \emph{branch} (\S\,The Verifier Ladder).
\item A cross-domain measurement of over-acceptance on two independent axes---wrong oracle ($99.6\%$) and
too-weak rung ($92\%$)---mirrored in SAT and reproduced on a real LLM code verifier (HumanEval+).
\item A provably sound ($\epsilon{=}0$) cheapest-first routing cascade, with a finite-sample risk analysis of
when relaxing onto cheaper rungs is admissible.
\item \textbf{Cost-repair in a real RLVR loop}: GRPO on Qwen2.5-3B/7B and Llama-3.1-8B, verifier as sole
variable; the sound cascade matches the strong verifier's quality at \mSevenBSavings\%/\longSavings\% fewer
strong-calls, the cheap reward fails to transfer while gaming rises, and the saving decays as the policy
strengthens---plus a continuous dial tracing the frontier.
\end{itemize}

\includegraphics[width=0.82\textwidth]{f_framework.pdf}
\caption{\textbf{One problem induces a family of decidable verifiers.} A nested strictness ladder
($\match\!\supseteq\!\umfe\!\supseteq\!\pfe$) on the objective-aware oracle, plus a separate \emph{branch}
for an out-of-domain oracle that cannot represent the objective. ``Solved'' is whichever node one selects.
Determinism does not prevent over-acceptance on two axes---a wrong (out-of-domain) oracle (Axis~1,
$99.6\%$) and a too-weak rung (Axis~2, $92\%$). We price the family, dial it continuously, and route it
soundly---then do so \emph{inside} an RLVR loop.}\label{fig:framework}
\end{figure*}
